first-author h-index

Properties

  • Metric Type: Core Property
  • Considerations and Adjustments: Coauthorship
  • Publication Focus: Core Publications
  • Citation Focus: Core Citations

Description

The first-author h-index (Butson and Yu 2010) was designed to rescale outputbetween large and small collaborative research teams under an assumption that larger teams could produce more output per year just by the nature of being larger. It attempts to rescale the h-index based on the number of publications in the h-core that were first-authored (Pfa).

$$h_{fa}=h \frac{P_h + P_{fa}}{P_h}=h + P_{fa}.$$

The authors did not seem to realize that the number of papers in the core Ph is, by definition, equal to h and thus some of the terms cancel, leaving the metric just the sum of h and the number of first-authored papers that make up h. This index ranges from equal to the h-index if the investigator is never a first author of publications in the h-core to double the h-index if they are the first author of every publication in the core.

This is conceptually similar to some other metrics such as the stratified h-index and the hmajor-index.

iterative weighted EM-index

Properties

  • Metric Type: Alternative Metric
  • Publication Focus: Core Publications
  • Citation Focus: Core Citations

Description

The iterative weighted EM-index (Bihari et al. 2021) is a modification of the EM-index which uses a weighted-sum of each successive element in the vector rather than the square-root of the sum. The index begins by creating a vector (E) which is equivalent to the upper/excess half of the two-sided h-index, namely a series of h-index values calculated from the citation curve of just the core publications, stopping when one reaches only a single remaining publication, no citations remain, or all remaining publications have only a single citation. From this vector, iwEM can be calculated as:

$$iw_{EM}=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\frac{E_i}{i},$$

where Ei and n are the ith element and length of E, respectively.

Example

Publications are ordered by number of citations, from highest to lowest. After each step, Ei is subtracted from the citations of the top Ei publications. All publications beyond the top Ei are ignored at subsequent steps.

Rank (i)123456789101112131415161718

Adjusted Citations (Ci)4313400
Rank (i)12345
E3 = 3
Adjusted Citations (Ci)40101
Rank (i)123
E4 = 2
Adjusted Citations (Ci)388
Rank (i)12
E5 = 2
Adjusted Citations (Ci)366
Rank (i)12
E6 = 2
Adjusted Citations (Ci)344
Rank (i)12
E7 = 2
Adjusted Citations (Ci)322
Rank (i)12
E8 = 2

iwEM is the sum of each component of E weighted by it's order, thus iwEM = 6/1 + 5/2 + 3/3 + 2/4 + 2/5 + 2/6 + 2/7 + 2/8 = 11.3802

iterative weighted EM′-index

Properties

  • Metric Type: Alternative Metric
  • Publication Focus: All Publications
  • Citation Focus: All Citations

Description

The iterative weighted EM′-index (Bihari et al. 2021) is a modification of the EM′-index (Bihari and Tripathi 2017) which uses a weighted-sum of each successive element in the vector rather than the square-root of the sum. It is an extension of the iterative weighted EM-index which includes all publications, rather than just those from the core. We begin by creating a vector (E) where the first value is E1 = h. Subsequent values of the vector, Ei+1, are determined by subtracting Ei from the citation count for all publications in the core defined by Ei, and recalculating h from these new citation counts, reranking all publications by these new citation counts as necessary (i.e., some of the publications previously in the tail of the citation distribution may advance beyond publications in the core as citations representing earlier calculations of h are “used up”). This process continues until one runs out of citations, all of the remaining publications have only a single remaining citation, or there is only a single publication left to be considered. From this vector, one calculates the index as:

$$iw_{EM^\prime}= \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\frac{E_i}{i},$$

where Ei and n are the ith element and length of E, respectively.

o-index

Properties

  • Metric Property: Compound Metric
  • Publication Focus: Core Publications
  • Citation Focus: Core Citations

Description

The o-index (Dorogovtsev and Mendses 2015) was designed to balance a researcher's most-cited work with their diligence in regular publication, and is simply the geometric mean of their h-index and the count of citations to their most cited work. It is calculated as:

$$o=\sqrt{hC_{max}}.$$

discounted h-index

Properties

  • Metric Type: Core Metric
  • Considerations and Adjustments: Self-Citation
  • Publication Focus: All Publications, Core Publications
  • Citation Focus: All Citations, Core Citations

Description

The discounted h-index (Ferrara and Romero 2013) was designed to adjust the h-index for self-citations by multiplying it by square-root of the percentage of total citations that were not self-citations. It is readily calculated as:

$$dh=h \sqrt{\frac{C^P-S^P}{C^P}},$$

where SP is the sum of self-citations for all publications.

Year-based EM-index by publications

Properties

  • Metric Type: Alternative Metric
  • Considerations and Adjustments: Time
  • Publication Focus: All Publications

Description

The Year-based EM-index by publications (Bihari and S. Tripathi 2018) is an adapation of the EM-index applied to the career years h-index by publications. This metric is a measure of publication intensity or distribution, rather than citation intensity as captured by most h-index type indices. Rather than create a list of publications ranked by citation count, one creates a list of years ranked by publication count. This list is then processed in the same multivariate manner as the EM-index.

Example

Years are ordered by number of publications, from highest to lowest. After each step, Ei is subtracted from the publications of the top Ei years. All years beyond the top Ei are ignored at subsequent steps.

Rank (i)12345
E1 = 3
Adjusted Publications (Pi)321
Rank (i)123
E2 = 2

The sum of the 2 E values is 5. The Year-based EM-index by publications is the square-root of this sum, thus Yp_EM = 2.4495.

Properties

  • Metric Type: Alternative Metric
  • Considerations and Adjustments: Time
  • Publication Focus: All Publications
  • Citation Focus: All Citations

Description

The Year-based EM-index by publication year citations (Bihari and S. Tripathi 2018) is an adapation of the EM-index applied to the career years h-index by citations. This metric is a measure of citation intensity or distribution by publication year, rather than by publication. Rather than create a list of publications ranked by citation count, one creates a list of years ranked by citation count for all publications from that year. This list is then processed in the same multivariate manner as the EM-index.

Example

Years are ordered by number of citations, from highest to lowest. After each step, Ei is subtracted from the citations of the top Ei years. All years beyond the top Ei are ignored at subsequent steps.

Rank (i)123

Rank (i)123
E4 = 3
Adjusted Citations (Ci)9042
Rank (i)123
E5 = 2
Adjusted Citations (Ci)882
Rank (i)12

The sum of the 6 E values is 17. Year-based EM-index by publication year citations is the square-root of this sum, thus Ypc_EM = 4.2426.

h′-index

Properties

  • Metric Type: Core Property
  • Publication Focus: All Publications
  • Citation Focus: All Citations, Core Citations, Tail Citations

Description

The h′-index (Zhang 2013) is a variant of the h-index, where h is scaled by the ratio of excess and tail citations relative to the core. It is measured as:

$$h^\prime=\frac{eh}{t}.$$

where e is the e-index (the square root of the count of citations in the core above and beyond what is necessary to produce h) and t is the square root of all citations for publications in the tail (i.e., not in the core).

hc

Properties

  • Metric Type: Core Property
  • Publication Focus: Core Publications
  • Citation Focus: Core Citations

Description

hc (Kharana and Sharma 2022) is a modification of the h-index which includes an additional weighting factor for the most cited publication of the author's record. This extra factor is the maximum power one can raise h to which is less than the maximum citations, which is then added to h, thus:

$$h_c = h+k.$$

The original authors describe the calculation of k through an algorithm, but as long as h > 1 it can directly be determined as:

$$k = \left[\log_h\left(C_{\max}-1 \right)\right],$$

which is the logarithm in base h of one less than the largest number of citations to a single paper, truncated to an integer. If h ≤ 1, then hc = 2 if the maximum citations is greater than one, otherwise hc = h.

k-index (Anania and Caruso)

Properties

  • Metric Type: Core Metric
  • Publication Focus: Core Publications
  • Citation Focus: Core Citations

Description

The k-index (Anania and Caruso 2013) is a variant of the h-index, where h includes a fractional component representing the proportion of the Hirsch core citations (CH) which are above and beyond those necessary to achieve h, making k essentially a function of h and the e-index. It can be calculated as:

$$k=h+\left(1-\frac{h^2}{C^H}\right)=h+\frac{e^2}{C^H}=h+\frac{e^2}{h^2 + e^2}.$$

k will always be between h and h+1. The authors also described a very similar metric known as the w-index (Anania and Caruso); w will always be equal to or greater than k.

w-index (Anania and Caruso)

Properties

  • Metric Type: Core Metric
  • Publication Focus: All Publications
  • Citation Focus: All Citations, Core Citations

Description

The w-index (Anania and Caruso 2013) is a variant of the h-index, where h includes a fractional component representing the proportion of the total citations (CT) which are above and beyond those necessary to achieve h. It can be calculated as:

$$w=h+\left(1-\frac{h^2}{C_T}\right).$$

w will always be between h and h+1. The authors also described a very similar metric known as the k-index (Anania and Caruso); w will always be equal to or greater than k.

h-norm index

Properties

  • Metric Type: Core Metric
  • Considerations and Adjustments: Coauthorship
  • Publication Focus: Core Publications
  • Citation Focus: Core Citations

Description

The h-norm index (Anania and Caruso 2013) is described more or less incidentally when building up to normalized versions of other metrics in the paper. It is a version of the h-index normalized by the number of coauthors for each publication. It is very similar to the calculation of he when determining the adapted pure h-index (fractional credit), but citation counts are divided by the number of coauthors rather than the square root. Citation accounts are adjusted for coauthor counts as:

$$C^{*}_i = \frac{C_i}{A_i}.$$

and h-norm isdetermined using these adjusted counts:

$$h{-}norm = \underset{i}{\max}\left(i \leq C^{*}_i\right).$$

Example

Publications are ordered by adjusted number of citations, from highest to lowest.

Citations (Ci)541024151131144112100000
Authors (Ai)313231444114242111
Adjusted Citations (\(C^*_i\))18.0010.008.007.503.673.002.751.001.001.001.000.500.500.000.000.000.000.00
Rank (i)123456789101112131415161718
h-norm = 4

The largest rank where \(i \leq C^*_i\) is 4.

k-norm index

Properties

  • Metric Type: Core Metric
  • Considerations and Adjustments: Coauthorship
  • Publication Focus: Core Publications
  • Citation Focus: Core Citations

Description

The k-norm index (Anania and Caruso 2013) is a variant of the k-index (Anania and Caruso), where citation counts are first normalized by dividing by the number of coauthors for each publication:

$$C^{*}_i = \frac{C_i}{A_i}.$$

These are used to calculate a normalized version of h (h-norm index), and then k-norm is determined as:$$k{-}norm=h{-}norm+\left(1-\frac{{h{-}norm}^2}{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{h{-}norm} C^{*}_i}\right).$$

yearly h-index

Properties

  • Metric Type: Core Metric
  • Considerations and Adjustments: Time
  • Publication Focus: Core Publications
  • Citation Focus: Core Citations

Description

The yearly h-index (Singh 2022) is described more or less incidentally when building up to another metric in the paper. It is simply the average h-index for a researcher based on calculations of h from sets of papers published from each individual year of their career, rather than a single h determined for the entire career. It is calculated as:

$$\bar{h}_y = \frac{\sum\limits_{i=Y_0}^{Y}h_i}{\text{academic age}},$$

where hi is simply an h-index calculated only for papers from year i. Regardless of citation counts, the yearly h- index will always be limited by the total number of papers published per year, thus highly cited papers and poorly cited papers will frequently contribute about equal weight in any given year. It serves more as a general measure of consistency and—assuming most papers get at least a few citations—is little different than the average number of papers published per year, at least for most individuals.

t-index (Singh)

Properties

  • Metric Type: Alternative Metric
  • Considerations and Adjustments: Time
  • Publication Focus: All Publications, Core Publications
  • Citation Focus: All Citations, Core Citations

Description

The t-index (Singh 2022) is an alternative metric for impact based on the information entropy of individual publications, with scaling factors based on academic age and the yearly h-index. It is calculated as:

$$t=4e^{T/T^\prime}\bar{h}_y,$$

where

$$T = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{P}\frac{c_i}{C^P}\ln\frac{c_i}{C^P}$$

and

$$T^\prime=\ln \left(10 \times \text{academic age} \right).$$

It is a bit difficult to interpret and is not guaranteed to monotonically increase.

  • Citation Focus: All Citations

Description

Fairness (Prathap 2014; Gagolewski et al. 2022) is a measure of the distribution of citations across all of an author's publications. A value of 1 would indicate that all publications have the same number of citations, while lower values indicate a skewed distribution with some publications having more citations than other. It is calculated as:

$$\eta = \frac{\left(C^P\right)^2}{P\sum\limits_{i=1}^{P} C_i^2}.$$

It is not generally considered as an impact measure in-and-of itself, but serves as a complement to other metrics.

Zynergy-Index

Properties

  • Publication Focus: All Publications

Description

The Zynergy-Index (Prathap 2014) is a heuristic alternative to the h-index based on a thermodynamical model. It is a function of the total number of citations and publications of an author, along with the distribution of the citations across the publications as measured by fairness (η).

$$z = \sqrt[3]{\frac{\eta \left(C^P\right)^2}{P}}$$.

3DSI (ρR)

Properties

  • Metric Type: Alternative Metric
  • Metric Property: Multidimensional Metric
  • Publication Focus: All Publications
  • Citation Focus: All Citations

Description

Siudem et al. (2020) describe a three-dimensional model to measure scientific impact of an author, generally called 3DSI. The first dimension is simply the total number of publications, and the second is the total number of citations. The third dimension is for a parameter ρ which generally describes the distribution of citations within the publications based on a preferential attachment rule (strictly speaking ρ is the ratio of preferential citations to total citations). Roughly speaking, positive values of ρ (approximately one or greater) indicate that most citations are preferentially going to a limited number of publications, values around zero indicate approximately a random citation distribution according to their model, and negative values indicate citations are more evenly spread among publications.

While the first two dimensions are simple to calculate, there are many methods for estimating ρR from empirical data.

In this version, we use a rank-size domain estimator, ρR (Gagolewski et al. 2022), determined as:

$$\rho_R = \frac{P-\frac{2csr^3}{C^P}+1}{P-\frac{csr^3}{C^P}},$$

where csr is the cube-root of the sum of ranks.

partnership ability

Properties

  • Metric Type: Basic Statistic
  • Considerations and Adjustments: Coauthorship
  • Publication Focus: All Publications

Description

The partnership ability index (Schubert 2012) is the collaborator equivalent of the h-index. It is the largest value for which φ coauthors of the target author have produced at least φ publications with the target author.

A φ of zero would indicate the target author has only produced solo-author publications. A φ of one indicates at least one coauthor on one publication, but also at most one coauthor with whom they have published more than once.

φ is essentially a simple form of a collaboration network metric.

stratified h-index

Properties

  • Metric Type: Core Metric
  • Metric Property: Multidimensional Metric
  • Considerations and Adjustments: Coauthorship
  • Publication Focus: Core Publications

Description

The stratified h-index (Würtz and Schmidt 2016) attempts to deal with coauthorship by producing a set of h-indices based on differing authorship position wihin the publications. Essentially, in addition to the general h-index, one calculates independent indices for publications in which one is the first author, second author, third author, or last author, with these four positions being deemed the highest contributing to a publication, in various degrees of importance. In theory, by viewing this set of indices, rather than a single value, one can determine how much of an author's impact is based on “primary” contributions to publications versus secondary.

This concept is very similar to a few other proposals, including the hmajor-index and the first-author h-index.

The platinum h-index (Smith 2015) is a compound metric that rescales the h-index based on the academic age of the researcher and the average number of citations per publication. It is simply calculated as:

stochastic h-index

Properties

  • Metric Type: Core Metric
  • Publication Focus: Core Publications
  • Citation Focus: Core Citations

Description

The stochastic h-index (Naid and Turlach 2012) is a variant of the h-index where h is modified to include a fractional component equal to the probability that it will increase by at least one by the next year. It is somewhat similar to the rational h-index and the real h-index in that its value ranges between h and h+1 and that the fractional component indicates something about progress toward the higher value.

Although the logic behind this metric is not particularly difficult, the calculation is a bit complicated to explain. Publications can be divided into two sets: those already with h+1 or more citations (thus not needing any additional citations for the researcher to reach the next value of h) and those with h or fewer citations. The number of publications in each of these sets are labeled as L0 and n, respectively. The number of publications within the second set that will need to gain citations to reach h+1 is k = h−L0

The probability that one of the publications in the second set will get to h+1 citations is determined from a Poisson distribution with a mean equal to the average annual citation rate of that publication (λi) and the number of citations it needs to gain to reach h+1. The probability it will reach at least h+1 citations is labeled pi, and the probability it will not reach at least h+1 citations is labeled qi = 1−pi.

If a publication has zero citations, its presumed rate of future citation is based on the age of the publication, determined as:

$$\lambda_i=-ln\left(\frac{\text{age}_i+1}{\text{age}_i+2}\right).$$

Give the probabilities of the individual publications reaching at least h+1 citations in the next year, the stochastic h-index is then calculated as

$$h_s=h + 1 - \sum\limits_{i=1}^k Q_i,$$

where

$$Q_0=\prod\limits_{i=1}^{n}q_i \\Q_1=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\left(p_i\prod\limits_{j=1, j\ne i}^{n}q_j\right) \\Q_2=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\sum\limits_{j=i+1}^{n}\left(p_ip_j\prod\limits_{k=1, k\ne i, k\ne j}^{n}q_k\right)\\\text{etc.}$$

These products and sums represent the combined probabilities of all of the ways that the publication set can fail to reach the citation count necessary to achieve an h-index of h+1.

One of the interesting factors of this index is it can, within certain limits, decrease from one year to the next. If more poorly cited publications fail to be cited with enough frequency in a given year, the reduced average rate of citation for those publications can decreases the probability of achieving h+1 the following year.

multiple h-index

Properties

  • Metric Type: Core Metric
  • Publication Focus: All Publications
  • Citation Focus: All Citations

Description

The multiple h-index (Yaminfirooz and Gholinia 2015) is essentially a function of the multidimensional h-index where the series of h-indices are used to combine the citation counts of individual publications into a single value, including a scaling for the age of each publication.

The first step is to calculate the multidimensional h-index, keeping track of which value of h in the multidimensional vector each publication falls into. From these, one can calculate the multiple h-index as

$$Mh = \sqrt{\sum\limits_{i=1}^P\frac{h_iC_i^2}{\text{age}_i}} = \sqrt{\sum\limits_{i=1}^P\frac{h_iC_i^2}{Y_i-Y_0+1}},$$

where hi is the value of the multidimensional h-index associated with the ith publication.

total publications (fractional counting)

Properties

  • Metric Type: Basic Statistic
  • Considerations and Adjustments: Coauthorship
  • Publication Focus: All Publications

Description

In just the same way one can account for coauthorship when calculating various citation-based metrics, one could use the same approach for counting the total number of publications of an author.

This version uses the fractional approach for assigning authorship credit, with each author of a publication getting an equal amount of credit. If Aiis the number of authors of the ith publication, the total publications of an author with fractional authorship counting is

$$P_{frac} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^P\frac{1}{A_i}.$$

In just the same way one can account for coauthorship when calculating various citation-based metrics, one could use the same approach for counting the total number of publications of an author.

L-Sequence

Properties

  • Metric Type: Core Metric
  • Metric Property: Multidimensional Metric
  • Considerations and Adjustments: Time
  • Publication Focus: Core Publications
  • Citation Focus: Core Citations

Description

The L-Sequence is a multi-dimensional measure where impact is measured as a series of h-indices with each one based on the citations for a single year. In practice, this means that from one year to the next, the only change in the sequences is the value for the latest year.

In practice the value of L for a particular year may be higher or lower than the previous year, depending on what the citation pattern for that particular year ended up being.

L∝

Properties

  • Metric Type: Core Metric
  • Considerations and Adjustments: Time
  • Publication Focus: Core Publications
  • Citation Focus: Core Citations

Description

L∝ is simply the sum of the values in the L-Sequence, meant to be viewed as an alternative to the h-index.

k-index (Kaptay)

Properties

  • Metric Type: Alternative Metric
  • Considerations and Adjustments: Coauthorship
  • Publication Focus: All Publications
  • Citation Focus: All Citations

Description

The k-index (Kapatay 2010) is a measure of impact that account for all citations as well as the number of authors of each publication. It is the square-root of the author-credit-adjusted citation count for each publication. Without additional information on author credit, credit is assigned strictly based on the fractional number of authors.

$$k=\sqrt{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{P}{\frac{C_i}{A_i}}}.$$

This metric is simply the square-root of the weighted citation aggregate (fractional), but is supposed to approximate the value of the h-index.

Kz index

Properties

  • Metric Type: Alternative Metric
  • Considerations and Adjustments: Time
  • Publication Focus: All Publications
  • Citation Focus: All Citations

Description

The Kz index (Sharma and Uddin, 2026) expands upon the two-dimensional interpretation of the h-index by introducing the age of publications and a measure of the impact of each publication to h into a three-dimensional framework which includes all publications, rather than just the core. The impact parameter for each publication is calculated as

$$k_i=\frac{\ln{C_i}}{\ln \left(h+1\right)}.$$

The metric Kz is then determined as

$$K_z=\sum\limits_{i=1}^P \frac{k_i}{Y - Y_i + 1},$$

where Y is the current year (the denominator is the age of the ith publication). This metric is essentially the area under a three-dimensional surface defined by the rank of each publication along one axis, it's age on a second axis, and the ratio of it's age-normalized impact on the third axis.
